prepare.detail: Note where the tires are wearing, when the car pulls, and whether steering or suspension work has recently been done. Keep any previous alignment readings.

prepare.title: Start with a sound car
prepare.detail: Use the correct cold tire pressures and tire sizes. Check for damage, uneven loading and worn or loose steering and suspension components before measuring.

prepare.title: Arrange an alignment system
prepare.detail: This job uses a level alignment platform and calibrated equipment. An alignment shop can supply measured before-and-after values and carry out any necessary adjustments.

steps.title: Separate the symptom from the diagnosis
steps.body: A car that pulls is giving you a clue, not an automatic alignment verdict. Use the suspension diagnosis article to work through loading, tires, brake drag and steering condition before deciding which angle is wrong.

steps.title: Measure all relevant angles before adjusting
steps.body: With the car set up according to the equipment instructions, record front and rear readings against the specification for its fitted suspension. Keep the steering wheel centered. Looking at all four wheels helps avoid correcting the front while overlooking the rear.

steps.title: Make only the adjustment the readings support
steps.body: Front toe is adjusted at the tie rods; rear toe uses the toe-link adjustment. The steering bellows must not twist as the front tie rods turn. The rear adjustment area must be clean so the hardware clamps correctly. Use the linked procedure for the actual movement and tightening steps.

steps.title: Treat camber correction as its own job
steps.body: Changing camber can also alter toe, so toe needs another check afterward. Rear camber has a control-arm adjustment. The linked front-camber correction involves special service fasteners and modification at the strut mounting hole; it is an advanced repair decision for a suitably equipped shop, not a bolt to loosen experimentally.

steps.title: Verify after final tightening
steps.body: Recheck the readings after the fasteners are tightened to their procedure-specific values. The wheels can move as the joints clamp. Save the final readings, then confirm straight-ahead steering and the original complaint on a controlled road test.

steps.title: Follow up on the tire wear
steps.body: Record the present wear pattern so the next inspection can show whether it is progressing. Existing damage will not disappear after adjustment. If the car still pulls with correct readings, continue the tire, brake and steering diagnosis instead of pushing the alignment outside specification.

watchFor.title: Alignment will not hold
watchFor.body: Loose joints, damaged components or a clamping problem need correction before another adjustment is likely to last.

watchFor.title: An angle outside the available adjustment
watchFor.body: Check ride height and component condition. Do not substitute arbitrary settings or modify suspension parts simply to make a display turn green.

watchFor.title: A changed suspension setup
watchFor.body: Factory alignment specifications are not automatically suitable for aftermarket suspension and wheel changes.

notes: This guide explains the inspection and planning sequence. The linked adjustment articles carry the fastener requirements and exact work steps.
Do not confuse wheel balancing with alignment: balancing addresses rotating mass; alignment addresses wheel direction and lean.

procedures.purpose: Work through pulling, tire wear, ride height and suspension condition before an adjustment.
Adjust front toe and protect the steering bellows while turning the tie rods.
Adjust rear toe, keep the clamping surfaces clean and verify the final readings.
Correct rear camber and recheck rear toe afterward.
Review the specialist front-camber correction and its required service fasteners.

guides.title: Bleed the MT82 clutch hydraulic circuit

applicability.equipment: MT82 six-speed manual transmission only; not the automatic transmission or the 5.2L/TR-3160 clutch system.

guides.summary: Use Ford’s reservoir-vacuum sequence to remove trapped air after hydraulic repair or diagnosis, then check pedal feel, clutch-pedal reserve and normal operation.
guides.introduction: A soft clutch pedal makes every shift feel like a negotiation with an unreasonable gearbox. I want a dependable response from the top of the pedal stroke. The MT82 clutch controls include the pedal, master cylinder, hydraulic tubes and slave cylinder; this job bleeds that circuit through the brake/clutch reservoir. [Component locations](#/document/G1704357) [Bleeding procedure](#/document/G1704358)
guides.why: Air and low fluid are possible causes of a soft pedal, clutch drag—where the clutch does not fully release—and difficult or grinding shifts. Leaking cylinders and damaged clutch parts can produce similar symptoms, so bleeding is a treatment for an identified hydraulic problem, not a damn parts lottery. Ford specifically requires bleeding after clutch-master-cylinder installation. [Clutch diagnosis](#/document/G1687369) [Master-cylinder installation](#/document/G1687295)

when.summary: After MT82 clutch hydraulic repair, or when diagnosis identifies trapped air causing poor release or a soft pedal.
notes: The clutch-master-cylinder installation procedure explicitly calls for hydraulic bleeding. The MT82 diagnostic chart also calls for it when air is involved in clutch drag, difficult shifting or an unusually soft pedal.
There is no fixed clutch-fluid flush interval established by these repair instructions. This guide does not apply to the 5.2L/TR-3160 system.

prepare.title: Confirm the car and the reason for bleeding
prepare.detail: This guide retains the 2015 2.3L, 3.7L and 5.0L scope with a confirmed MT82 six-speed manual transmission. Automatic transmissions and the 5.2L/TR-3160 application are outside this article. Use the procedure after hydraulic repair or when diagnosis identifies air; investigate fluid loss and repair leaks first. [MT82 bleeding](#/document/G1704358) [Clutch diagnosis](#/document/G1687369)

prepare.title: Gather the vacuum equipment
prepare.detail: Have Vacuum Pump Kit 416-D002, a suitable brake/clutch bleeder/filler kit and a tightly fitting reservoir stopper. Ford permits an alternative connection made from a 50 mm (1.96 in) rubber stopper with an 8 mm (0.31 in) pipe inserted through it. The gauge must allow you to read 15–20 inches of vacuum. Although the equipment list calls the bleeder/filler a pressure unit, this sequence applies vacuum at the reservoir. [Equipment and connection](#/document/G1704358)

prepare.title: Have the correct fluid and spill cleanup ready
prepare.detail: Use Motorcraft DOT 4 LV High Performance Motor Vehicle Brake Fluid, PM-20, meeting WSS-M6C65-A2. Read the product label and safety information before handling it; improper chemical handling can cause serious injury. Protect painted and plastic surfaces and keep water available to wash off any spill immediately. [Fluid and handling precautions](#/document/G1704358)

prepare.title: Prepare access and prevent an unexpected start
prepare.detail: You need access to the brake/clutch reservoir opening and the clutch pedal. The bleeding sequence does not require removing the pedal assembly, master cylinder, wheels or transmission. Keep the ignition off and the key out during service; disable remote start through Vehicle settings > Remote Start Setup if fitted. Wear eye and ear protection during vehicle service. Unexpected starting can cause serious injury. [Bleeding access and sequence](#/document/G1704358) [Service precautions](#/document/G1693189)

prepare.title: Prepare for the running reserve test
prepare.detail: Have a cable tie and tape measure for the clutch-pedal reserve check. The test uses first gear and slowly engages the clutch until initial forward movement or a noticeable rpm drop, so choose a clear area where that movement can be safely controlled. Keep people and obstacles out of the vehicle’s path. [Reserve-test method](#/document/G1687369)

steps.title: Check the circuit and let the pedal rise fully
steps.body: Confirm that all hydraulic tubes are correctly seated. Inspect the accessible hydraulic connections for leakage, especially where repairs were made, and resolve any leak before continuing. If the reservoir level is low, inspect both the clutch and brake systems. Check that the floor mat does not restrict the clutch pedal, then leave the pedal in its highest position. [Bleeding setup](#/document/G1704358) [Hydraulic and pedal checks](#/document/G1687369)

steps.title: Open the reservoir and fill to MAX
steps.body: Remove the brake/clutch reservoir cap and fill to the MAX mark with Motorcraft PM-20 DOT 4 LV fluid meeting WSS-M6C65-A2. MAX is the specified starting level for this service. Avoid spilling fluid; immediately wash any off painted or plastic surfaces with water to prevent damage. [Reservoir level and fluid](#/document/G1704358)

steps.title: Fit the sealed vacuum connection
steps.body: Connect the vacuum pump and suitable bleeder equipment to the rubber stopper, then fit the stopper tightly into the reservoir opening. Alternatively, use the specified 50 mm (1.96 in) stopper with an 8 mm (0.31 in) pipe through it. Hold the stopper in place for the vacuum operation. [Stopper and pump setup](#/document/G1704358)

steps.title: Draw vacuum, hold it and release it quickly
steps.body: With the stopper held in place, operate the pump until the gauge reads 15–20 inches of vacuum. Hold that vacuum for one minute, then quickly relieve it. Remove the stopper and vacuum equipment after releasing the vacuum. This is the specified vacuum sequence; do not substitute a brake-bleeding pressure setting. [Vacuum level and timing](#/document/G1704358)

steps.title: Restore the level and install the cap
steps.body: Check the reservoir level again and add the specified fluid to MAX. Install the reservoir cap before working the pedal. [Refill and cap sequence](#/document/G1704358)

steps.title: Cycle the clutch pedal and assess its feel
steps.body: Press and release the clutch pedal 10–12 times, or until the effort is consistent and positive at the top of its travel. Pay attention to the beginning of each press: you are looking for a repeatable response rather than a changing soft section. [Pedal cycling and endpoint](#/document/G1704358)

steps.title: Repeat the complete cycle as directed
steps.body: Repeat steps 3–6 two additional times, or until the pedal effort is consistent and positive at the top of travel. Each repeat includes fitting the stopper, drawing and holding 15–20 inches of vacuum for one minute, quickly releasing it, removing the equipment, refilling to MAX, installing the cap and cycling the pedal. If pedal effort remains inconsistent after the prescribed sequence, investigate the hydraulic fault before continuing. [Repeat sequence](#/document/G1704358) [Persistent soft-pedal diagnosis](#/document/G1687369)

steps.title: Set up the clutch-pedal reserve measurement
steps.body: Confirm that the reservoir cap is installed and remove the bleeding equipment from the work area. Attach a cable tie to the lower clutch pedal and attach the tape measure to the tie. Make sure the pedal can still travel fully without floor-mat interference. Fully depress the clutch, start the vehicle and select first gear. With the pedal still fully depressed, record the distance from the pedal to the seam on the steering wheel. [Bleeding completion](#/document/G1704358) [Reserve-test setup](#/document/G1687369)

steps.title: Measure travel to the first sign of engagement
steps.body: While watching the tape measure, slowly release the clutch pedal. Note the point where the vehicle first starts moving forward or the tachometer shows a noticeable engine-rpm decrease. Compare the tape reading at that point with the fully depressed reading: the change represents the pedal travel to initial engagement, or clutch-pedal reserve. Ford accepts reserve of at least 1 in (25 mm). Less than 1 in (25 mm) requires further clutch/control diagnosis. The limit is a test result, not a pedal-adjustment instruction. [Reserve measurement and limits](#/document/G1687369)

steps.title: Remove the measuring aids and check operation
steps.body: Once the measurement is finished, secure the vehicle and switch the engine off before removing the tape measure and cable tie. Check that the reservoir cap is fitted and the work area is clear. Then check normal clutch operation, including release and gear selection. A passing reserve result does not excuse continuing drag, grinding or difficult shifting; those symptoms still need diagnosis. [Required operating check](#/document/G1704358) [Symptom decisions](#/document/G1687369)

watchFor.title: Fluid loss after filling
watchFor.body: A falling level calls for inspection of both the clutch and brake systems. Repair the cause instead of repeatedly topping up and bleeding. [Leak checks](#/document/G1687369)

watchFor.title: Fluid on paint or plastic
watchFor.body: Wash the affected surface immediately with water. Leaving brake fluid on it can cause surface damage. [Spill response](#/document/G1704358)

watchFor.title: Unexpected movement during the reserve check
watchFor.body: Initial forward movement is one of the test’s engagement indicators. Keep the path clear and perform the test only where you can control the vehicle safely. [Running reserve test](#/document/G1687369)

watchFor.title: Transmission noise or a suspected transmission-fluid leak
watchFor.body: Check transmission-fluid level before driving to investigate these concerns. Ford warns that driving with low transmission fluid can damage the gearbox. This is separate from the brake/clutch reservoir level. [Transmission inspection precautions](#/document/G1687369)

notes: For ordinary owner checks, fluid between MIN and MAX is within the normal range and does not require topping up. The MAX instruction here belongs to the bleeding procedure. Ford advises immediate service when the level is outside the normal range because system performance may be compromised. [Ford fluid-level guidance](https://www.fordservicecontent.com/Ford_Content/vdirsnet/OwnerManual/Home/Content?ProcUid=G1605311&Uid=G1642989&buildtype=web&countryCode=USA&div=f&languageCode=en&userMarket=usa&vFilteringEnabled=False&variantid=3259) [Bleeding level](#/document/G1704358)

Master-cylinder replacement requires bleeding afterward, but its pedal/bracket removal operations are not prerequisites for this reservoir service. [Master-cylinder procedure](#/document/G1687295) [Bleeding procedure](#/document/G1704358)

procedures.purpose: Reservoir-vacuum equipment, fluid specification, bleeding sequence and required completion checks.
Clutch-pedal reserve measurement, acceptance limit and relevant symptom decisions.
Identify the MT82 clutch-control components.
Establish the requirement to bleed after master-cylinder installation.
Task-relevant personal protection and prevention of unexpected starting.

stepGroups.title: Check and fill the circuit
stepGroups.summary: Resolve leakage, ensure full pedal travel and establish the starting fluid level.

stepGroups.title: Bleed through the reservoir
stepGroups.summary: Apply the specified vacuum, refill, cycle the pedal and repeat to the stated endpoint.

stepGroups.title: Verify the result
stepGroups.summary: Measure clutch-pedal reserve and confirm normal operation.

diagnostics.finding: Pedal feel is consistent and reserve is at least 1 in (25 mm).
diagnostics.meaning: The hydraulic system passes Ford’s reserve criterion. [Reserve criterion](#/document/G1687369)
diagnostics.next: Complete the normal-operation check; investigate any remaining clutch or shifting symptom on its own merits. [Completion check](#/document/G1704358)

diagnostics.finding: Reserve is below 1 in (25 mm), or a soft pedal and poor release remain.
diagnostics.meaning: The hydraulic result is not acceptable. Low fluid, air, master-cylinder leakage, and slave-cylinder leakage or binding are listed possibilities. [Hydraulic diagnosis](#/document/G1687369)
diagnostics.next: Recheck level and leakage, then arrange inspection of the master and slave cylinders as indicated. Do not treat more bleeding as proof that a leaking or binding component is sound. [Clutch symptom chart](#/document/G1687369)

diagnostics.finding: The pedal is unusually hard or binds.
diagnostics.meaning: Ford’s hard-effort path includes master-cylinder binding, pedal damage or binding, and pressure-plate wear or damage. [Hard-pedal diagnosis](#/document/G1687369)
diagnostics.next: Check for restricted pedal travel and arrange diagnosis of the indicated components rather than assuming trapped air. [Pedal and clutch checks](#/document/G1687369)

diagnostics.finding: Drag, grinding or difficult shifts continue after bleeding.
diagnostics.meaning: The symptom chart also identifies clutch-disc damage, pressure-plate damage and input-shaft/pilot-bearing binding as possible causes. [Poor-release diagnosis](#/document/G1687369)
diagnostics.next: Have the remaining symptom diagnosed before choosing a repair; this bleeding guide does not establish a need to remove the transmission or replace clutch parts. [Clutch symptom chart](#/document/G1687369)

diagnostics.finding: The clutch slips.
diagnostics.meaning: Slip has a separate diagnostic path involving hydraulic-tube damage, friction components and a slave cylinder that binds or fails to retract. [Slip diagnosis](#/document/G1687369)
diagnostics.next: Arrange the relevant inspections instead of using repeated bleeding as a slip repair. [Clutch symptom chart](#/document/G1687369)

verification.title: Reservoir closed and equipment removed
verification.body: Finish the bleeding sequence with the reservoir filled to MAX and its cap installed. Remove the vacuum setup and pedal-measuring aids. [Bleeding completion](#/document/G1704358) [Reserve-test equipment](#/document/G1687369)

verification.title: Pedal feel and reserve both pass
verification.body: Confirm consistent, positive effort at the top of pedal travel and measured reserve of at least 1 in (25 mm). Record the result so a future change has something concrete to be compared with. [Pedal-feel endpoint](#/document/G1704358) [Reserve limit](#/document/G1687369)

verification.title: Normal release without recurring fluid loss
verification.body: Confirm normal clutch operation and check for renewed leakage. Continued drag, grinding, difficult shifting or falling fluid level means the underlying concern remains. [Operating check](#/document/G1704358) [Clutch diagnosis](#/document/G1687369)

guides.title: Diagnose brake pulsation and disc runout
guides.summary: Separate normal ABS feedback from brake roughness, inspect disc and hub seating, and use the correct runout and thickness limits before choosing a repair.
guides.introduction: Runout is the side-to-side movement of an installed brake disc as it rotates. A disc, its mating surfaces and the way the wheel is tightened all contribute to the assembled result. Pulsation is a symptom rather than proof that a disc needs replacing: normal ABS operation, brake condition and suspension faults must be distinguished first.
guides.why: Replacing or machining a disc without checking how it seats can leave the underlying problem in place. The wheel-installation instructions specifically warn that incorrect tightening order can produce high disc runout and accelerate brake roughness. Measuring the installed assembly and checking its mounting surfaces makes the repair decision more useful than judging the disc by appearance alone.

when.summary: When braking repeatedly causes speed-related pedal pulsation, steering-wheel nibble or shudder outside normal ABS operation.
notes: The brake diagnostic chart distinguishes pulsation with ABS activity on loose, wet or snowy surfaces from a repeatable brake or suspension concern.
This is a condition-based diagnostic task, not a scheduled rotor-machining service. Noise alone is not a reason to machine a disc.

prepare.title: Record the symptom before disassembly
prepare.detail: Note whether vibration appears under braking or continues with the pedal released, and whether it is felt in the pedal, steering wheel or seat. Use the brake diagnostic chart to select the correct path and safe test conditions.

prepare.title: Identify the fitted brake package
prepare.detail: Select the actual front caliper and rear disc type before using thickness limits or removing parts. The specification table has different minimum disc thicknesses for the two-, four- and six-piston front systems and for solid versus vented rear discs.

prepare.title: Prepare measuring and support equipment
prepare.detail: Arrange a reliable installed-disc runout measurement with appropriate dial-indicator equipment and a disc-thickness measurement. Have proper lifting equipment, a torque wrench and a way to support a removed caliper without loading its hose.

prepare.title: Plan the measurement boundary
prepare.detail: The linked specifications give an installed-disc runout limit. They do not provide a separate hub-flange runout setup or tolerance, so do not condemn a hub by applying the disc limit to the bare hub.

steps.title: Confirm that the symptom needs brake diagnosis
steps.body: Follow the Brake System vibration pinpoint test. Normal ABS operation can cause hydraulic-unit noise and pedal pulsation during heavy braking or on low-grip surfaces. A repeatable speed-related nibble or shudder can involve brake or suspension components and needs the corresponding inspection.

steps.title: Inspect the mountings before blaming the disc
steps.body: Check the relevant suspension components and wheel installation. If a disc is removed, clean its mating surfaces with the specified brake-cleaning material and a wire brush as directed. Keep the caliper supported; never let it hang by its hose. Corrosion, dirt and incorrect seating must be addressed before relying on an assembled measurement.

steps.title: Record installed-disc runout against its own limit
steps.body: Have the installed disc measured with a repeatable, correctly secured gauge setup and record the indicated lateral movement. The listed maximum installed brake-disc runout is 0.05 mm (0.002 in). Treat that as an assembled-disc criterion, not a separate hub-flange tolerance. If the result is excessive, investigate seating and component condition rather than automatically replacing the hub.

steps.title: Check thickness and whether machining is permitted
steps.body: Measure disc thickness and compare it with the exact fitted-brake specification. Machining is not allowed for discs with cross-drilled friction surfaces. A disc must not be machined when its thickness is less than the minimum thickness plus 0.6 mm (0.0236 in). This machining allowance is separate from the final minimum-thickness limit.

steps.title: Choose a repair that addresses the measured condition
steps.body: Use the brake diagnosis and disc condition to decide whether cleaning and correct installation, disc replacement or permitted machining is appropriate. Where machining is selected, the procedure requires an on-vehicle lathe rather than a bench lathe; follow its complete setup, runout adjustment and post-cut thickness checks. Do not machine simply to treat squeal or other brake noise.

steps.title: Reassemble correctly and verify the original complaint
steps.body: Use the correct front or rear disc procedure, including fasteners that must be replaced. Clean the wheel and hub mating surfaces and tighten wheel nuts in the prescribed star pattern with clean, dry threads. Apply the brake pedal several times after disc work to verify operation, then complete the appropriate controlled road test. Recheck wheel-nut tightness within 100 mi (160 km) after wheel installation.

watchFor.title: Runout and thickness are different measurements
watchFor.body: A disc can meet one requirement and fail another. Keep the installed runout result, measured thickness and correct package-specific minimum together in the job record.

watchFor.title: Loose or damaged suspension parts
watchFor.body: The brake vibration pinpoint test checks suspension condition as well as discs. Correct the identified fault instead of repeatedly machining rotors.

watchFor.title: The wrong brake-package limit is used
watchFor.body: Match the front caliper and rear disc configuration before using thickness limits or choosing parts. Two-, four- and six-piston front brakes and solid versus vented rear discs do not all share the same minimum thickness.

watchFor.title: A hub is blamed without an applicable test
watchFor.body: No separate hub-flange runout limit is established by the linked material. Investigate seating and use an appropriate hub-specific diagnostic reference before condemning the hub.

notes: The 0.05 mm (0.002 in) value is the installed-disc limit; it must not be reused as a bare-hub tolerance. The machining article separately specifies the lathe’s adjustment conditions.
Use a suitably equipped brake shop for a reliable installed-disc measurement, and follow the complete linked procedure when carrying out the repair.

Installed-disc runout and fitted-brake minimum-thickness specifications.
Front-disc access, caliper support, mating-surface cleaning and reassembly.

Machining eligibility, on-vehicle lathe requirements and final thickness checks.

guides.title: Measure wheel vibration and match the tire to the rim
guides.summary: Use loaded road-force or radial-runout measurements to identify the high spot, reposition a tire when appropriate and finish with correct wheel-to-hub seating.
guides.introduction: A wheel-and-tire assembly can be balanced yet still feel rough because it is not perfectly round or does not deflect evenly under load. Balancing corrects uneven mass; runout and road-force testing investigate a different source of vibration. Match mounting changes the tire’s position on the rim so their combined variation can be reduced before parts are replaced.
guides.why: A loaded road-force test measures how the tire behaves against a roller, while an unloaded dial indicator measures its shape. The diagnostic procedure prefers loaded testing for judging tire serviceability. Careful marking and repeat measurements help distinguish a tire contribution from a wheel contribution, and proper hub seating prevents the final installation from introducing another offset.

when.summary: When diagnosis points to a wheel/tire vibration that persists after basic tire, pressure and wheel-condition checks.
notes: Do not perform this tire/wheel vibration diagnosis on tires with fewer than 200 mi (322 km) in service; initial flat spotting can change during that period. This does not postpone correcting obvious damage or unsafe tire condition.
Before runout matching, remove temporary flat spotting by driving 20 or more miles immediately before measurement, as directed in the matching procedure.
This is diagnostic correction when a concern is present, not a mileage-based tire-matching service.

prepare.title: Start with sound, correctly inflated tires
prepare.detail: Inspect for damage, bent wheels and loose fasteners, and use the recommended tire size and wheel specification. Set the specified pressure from the vehicle’s tire label using an accurate digital gauge. Keep each assembly’s vehicle position marked.

prepare.title: Use equipment that centers and protects the wheel
prepare.detail: Use the correct balancer adapters and clean assemblies. Incorrect centering can create an apparent runout problem. The wheel procedure requires suitable center-clamp tire-changing equipment and balancing equipment that does not contact the wheel face.

prepare.title: Choose the approved measurement and matching method
prepare.detail: Loaded Hunter Road Force measurement is preferred. A securely mounted dial indicator can measure radial runout at the center tread rib, but an unloaded reading alone cannot decide whether a tire should be removed from service.

prepare.title: Have TPMS-safe tire service and marking materials ready
prepare.detail: Prepare tire chalk or crayon, the tire-changing procedure, fast-drying, corrosion-inhibiting bead lubricant and wheel-installation instructions. Tire rotation on the rim must protect the pressure sensor and reseat the beads correctly.

steps.title: Measure and mark the baseline
steps.body: After the condition checks and flat-spot warm-up, mark the assembly’s vehicle position and measure using the correct adapters. Loaded road force above 20 lb (9 kg) calls for match mounting; a value at or below that limit leads to balancing and wheel-to-hub optimization. With the dial-indicator method, measure the center tread rib from its zeroed low spot through a complete revolution; assembly runout above 1.14 mm (0.045 in) calls for matching. Record the high spot and reading.

steps.title: Select the right matching path for the machine
steps.body: Use only the Ford-approved Hunter method described in Wheel to Tire Runout Minimization, or its manual matching sequence. Generation I/II machines supply readings only. Generation III uses “Match Without Rim Runout” when available; otherwise use the manual sequence. Generation IV/V uses “180 Matching.” Do not assume another automatic matching prompt is equivalent.

steps.title: Reposition the tire and take the second measurement
steps.body: For the manual method, place a reference mark on the tire at the valve stem, break the beads using the TPMS precautions, lubricate them as directed and rotate the tire 180 degrees on the wheel. The reference mark is now opposite the valve stem. Reinflate correctly and remeasure, marking the new high spot and reading. If the result is within the applicable limit, proceed to balancing and hub optimization.

steps.title: Use the high spots to choose the next branch
steps.body: If two above-limit measurements keep the high spots within 4 in (101.6 mm) of each other on the tire, the tire is the likely contributor; the procedure requires both measurements before that conclusion. If the second high spot is within 4 in (101.6 mm) of the opposite position of the first high spot on the wheel, inspect the bare wheel and measure its runout; the matching procedure specifies replacement above 1.14 mm (0.0449 in). If neither pattern fits and the result remains high, follow the illustrated 90-degree tire repositioning branch. Do not replace a tire merely because one unloaded reading was high.

steps.title: Balance the corrected assembly and optimize hub seating
steps.body: Permanently mark the final high spot and reading on the inner sidewall and balance the assembly. For wheel-to-hub optimization, place its high spot at 6 o’clock and hand-snug the nuts. Lower the tire until it just contacts the ground and slightly loads the suspension, then tighten as directed. During this specific optimization operation, do not let the full vehicle weight rest on the tire while tightening.

steps.title: Finish the installation and confirm the result
steps.body: Use the wheel procedure for clean mating surfaces, the specified torque and star pattern. Keep lubricant away from wheel-stud and wheel-nut threads and from brake friction surfaces. Verify whether the original vibration has improved and continue the diagnostic path if it has not. Recheck wheel-nut tightness within 100 mi (160 km) after installation.

watchFor.title: A false reading caused by setup
watchFor.body: Dirt, the wrong balancer adapter or movement of the dial-indicator stand can imitate an assembly fault. Confirm repeatable setup before making a parts decision.

watchFor.title: A tire condemned from unloaded runout alone
watchFor.body: The diagnostic instructions say unloaded runout cannot accurately determine tire serviceability. Loaded testing and the complete diagnostic branch matter.

watchFor.title: A wheel-to-hub exception is missed
watchFor.body: The runout-optimization procedure deliberately uses only slight tire loading while tightening. Keep that special instruction with this operation rather than blindly applying the general installation wording about the vehicle resting on its tires.

watchFor.title: Damage during tire service
watchFor.body: Use the TPMS precautions, approved wheel-clamping approach and appropriate lubricant. Correcting vibration is not a reason to risk a pressure sensor or wheel finish.

notes: Road-force and geometric runout use different units and answer different questions; 20 lb is a force threshold, not a tire-pressure setting.

The matching article rounds the bare-wheel limit to 0.0449 in while the diagnostic article gives 0.045 in for the assembly criterion; both metric values are 1.14 mm. Keep the wheel and assembly decisions in their respective branches.

guides.title: Parasitic battery drain: find what stays awake
guides.summary: Measure current after the car has settled, then isolate the circuit that is drawing too much instead of guessing at a module.
guides.introduction: Some electrical use continues after the ignition is switched off. The diagnostic question is whether the car settles to the expected resting draw, or whether a lamp, circuit or module keeps consuming too much. The tricky part is preserving the car’s state while measuring it: opening a circuit or waking a module can change the very behavior you are trying to observe.
guides.why: A current reading taken too soon can mistake normal module activity for a fault. A power interruption can also reset a troublesome module and temporarily hide the drain. A deliberate setup makes the final number meaningful.

when.summary: When a charged, tested battery repeatedly loses charge while the vehicle is parked.
notes: This is condition-based diagnosis, not a periodic maintenance service.
Do not begin with a discharged battery or an active low-battery message. Charge and test the battery first.

prepare.title: Prepare the correct measuring equipment
prepare.detail: The procedure specifies an inline ammeter capable of reading milliamps with a 10-amp capability, plus a 30-amp fused jumper used to preserve continuity during setup. A test lamp or voltage reading does not substitute for this current measurement.

prepare.title: Allow enough uninterrupted time
prepare.detail: Plan for at least 90 minutes of key-off settling, subject to equipment and regional differences, and for another settling period when the isolation procedure requires it.

prepare.title: Use the circuit information
prepare.detail: Have the fuse locations and relevant wiring information ready before beginning. A thermal camera can help identify activity, but the current measurement confirms the draw.

steps.title: Establish a sound starting point
steps.body: Fully charge and test the battery. Record the parking duration and conditions that lead to discharge. Follow the procedure’s activation drive—at least five minutes above 48 km/h (30 mph)—before setting up the resting test.

steps.title: Arrange access without keeping the car awake
steps.body: With ignition off, prepare hood, door-latch and fuse-box access exactly as the test describes so lamps do not remain on. Disable applicable approach or alarm features. On an automatic, verify that Park indication works; an incorrect indication can prevent modules from sleeping.

steps.title: Connect the meter without interrupting power
steps.body: Use the fused jumper and inline-meter connection sequence in Battery Drain Check. Lock the vehicle as directed and move all keys/fobs at least 50 feet away. If continuity is broken, or meter connections need changing, follow the jumper and power-down instructions rather than treating the earlier settling time as valid.

steps.title: Wait, then interpret the resting draw
steps.body: Keep the ignition off and allow at least 90 minutes for the modules to settle. Record the current. The procedure describes a 25–50 mA range depending on equipment and recommends comparison with a similar vehicle; one universal cutoff should not replace that context.

steps.title: Isolate the circuit, then the actual cause
steps.body: If draw is excessive, follow the staged fuse and component isolation sequence and note the current change. The first fuse that reduces the draw identifies a circuit, not automatically a failed component. Check whether a module is being kept awake by an input, and include aftermarket electrical connections when fitted.

steps.title: Finish the diagnosis and restore the vehicle
steps.body: If fused circuits do not explain the draw, follow the checks for other battery-fed circuits and the generator. Restore the test connections and equipment, carry out required window initialization, and verify that the excessive draw is gone after the prescribed settling period.

watchFor.title: The reading changes when you touch the setup
watchFor.body: A door event, key proximity or interrupted battery connection can change module activity. Restore the required test conditions before deciding a repair worked.

watchFor.title: A module appears to be the drain
watchFor.body: Investigate its inputs before replacing it. An input can keep an otherwise functioning module awake.

watchFor.title: Only a voltage reading is available
watchFor.body: Battery voltage alone does not locate a parasitic-current path; use the specified current test.

notes: This guide is an overview of an equipment-based electrical test. Keep the ignition off during the inline-current measurement. Never crank or start the engine, or switch on heavy electrical loads, with the inline ammeter connected. Follow the meter and fused-jumper sequence in the full procedure.

procedures.purpose: Perform the complete drain test, sleep preparation and circuit-isolation sequence.
Confirm battery condition before diagnosing an external drain.
Fully charge the battery before the drain test.
Identify the negative cable and use the proper disconnect/reconnect procedure.
Carry out the required one-touch window initialization after reconnection.
Review battery precautions before connecting test equipment.

guides.title: A/C odor: find the moisture source before treating the evaporator
guides.summary: Distinguish a brief musty start-up smell from a cabin water leak or another odor, then use the correct treatment when indicated.
guides.introduction: The timing of a smell is useful evidence. A musty burst when the A/C first starts is a different clue from a smell that remains all the time, wet carpeting, or an odor that appears only while passing through an outside source. Evaporator treatment is one possible repair. It is not a substitute for finding a fluid leak, drying a wet interior or clearing a drainage problem.
guides.why: Warmth and moisture can support growth in the A/C housing or in other wet parts of the cabin. Treating the wrong area may leave the cause untouched. The repair starts by locating the source, then dries and treats the evaporator only when the checks support that choice.

when.summary: When a recurring odor has been traced to the A/C system; treatment is based on the finding, not a fixed interval.
notes: A musty odor lasting about 30 seconds after A/C start-up is a useful clue in the procedure, not proof by itself.
An odor outside the A/C system calls for repair or cleaning of its actual source.

prepare.title: Describe when it happens
prepare.detail: Compare start-up versus continuous odor and fresh-air versus recirculation operation. Note moisture in the cabin and any relationship to weather.

prepare.title: Have the specified treatment equipment
prepare.detail: The treatment uses Motorcraft A/C Cooling Coil Coating YN-29 and the flexible applicator. The procedure approves that coating specifically; a different spray may damage the existing coating or worsen odor.

prepare.title: Plan access and drying
prepare.detail: The work includes blower removal, protection of nearby electronics and interior surfaces, and two specified drying/curing runs. Plan an outdoor or safely ventilated engine-running space; never run this drying cycle in a closed garage. Apply the parking brake and select Park or Neutral as appropriate. Follow the product precautions.

steps.title: Classify the odor before applying anything
steps.body: Separate chemical, outside-air, interior-generated and microbiological smells. Persistent chemical or fluid-like odors need their source investigated. Do not proceed with evaporator treatment when the source lies elsewhere.

steps.title: Check drainage and unwanted water
steps.body: Inspect the evaporator drain, both front carpets, blower area and cowl air inlet. Moisture in the carpets or blower area redirects the job toward water-leak diagnosis. Remove standing water or foreign material from the inlet as directed.

steps.title: Dry the A/C housing
steps.body: For a confirmed treatment, open the doors and windows. With A/C off, select register airflow, full warm and high blower speed; run the engine for 25 minutes, then switch the ignition off. Drying is a separate preparation step, not the coating application itself.

steps.title: Open the required access and protect the controls
steps.body: Remove the blower using its exact procedure. Remove an exposed blower speed control or resistor as directed; a control outside the housing and airflow does not need removal for that reason. Keep coating off the speed control and interior surfaces.

steps.title: Apply the specified coating to the evaporator face
steps.body: Fill the flexible applicator with one full bottle of YN-29. Insert its nozzle into the evaporator housing and direct the spray across the entire core face until the bottle is empty, following the treatment procedure.

steps.title: Reassemble and complete the cure
steps.body: Reinstall the removed blower and applicable control. Repeat the specified register/full-warm/high-blower, A/C-off run for 25 minutes, then switch the ignition off to complete the curing sequence. Reassess the original odor conditions rather than judging success only by a new fragrance.

watchFor.title: Wet carpet or moisture around the blower
watchFor.body: Investigate the water entry; the treatment procedure specifically redirects these findings away from an unnecessary evaporator coating.

watchFor.title: Odor returns after treatment
watchFor.body: Revisit drain restrictions, standing water and the original source classification instead of automatically adding another product.

watchFor.title: A smell that tracks an external location
watchFor.body: Recirculation may reduce outside odor, but treating the evaporator will not remove an external source.

notes: Blower removal provides treatment access; it does not mean the blower has failed.
No routine refrigerant recharge or annual chemical treatment is implied by this odor procedure.

procedures.purpose: Classify the odor and perform the complete inspection, coating and curing sequence.
Remove and install the blower motor for treatment access.
Remove and install the blower speed control when its exposure requires it.

guides.title: A/C performance and leak testing: measure before adding refrigerant
guides.summary: Use ambient conditions, both pressure readings and targeted leak tests to find why cooling is weak.
guides.introduction: Weak cooling has several possible paths: insufficient airflow through the condenser, a control or compressor problem, a restriction, or the wrong amount of refrigerant. Adding refrigerant before identifying the cause can create an overcharge without repairing anything. A useful test records how the system behaves under defined conditions, then follows the evidence to the appropriate repair.
guides.why: Pressure changes with outdoor temperature and operating conditions. A number from a single gauge means little without that context. The linked engine-specific tests use high- and low-side pressure charts together, so the result can guide diagnosis rather than guesswork.

when.summary: When cooling is weak, compressor operation is abnormal, or evidence suggests a refrigerant leak.
notes: This is condition-based testing and repair; there is no routine blind-recharge interval.
The performance test requires ambient temperature of at least 21°C (70°F). Use the procedure’s appropriate temperature and humidity chart.

prepare.title: Choose the engine-specific test
prepare.detail: Use the 2.3L, 3.7L or 5.0L refrigerant-system article that matches the vehicle. Record ambient temperature and the actual symptom.

prepare.title: Use appropriate service equipment
prepare.detail: The tests require an A/C service unit. Refrigerant identification, approved recovery/charging equipment and suitable leak-detection equipment are needed for the applicable follow-on work.

prepare.title: Protect eyes, skin and the work area
prepare.detail: Liquid refrigerant can injure eyes or freeze skin. Wear the specified eye protection and follow the refrigerant/equipment precautions. Run the engine only in a well-ventilated area with the parking brake applied and Park or Neutral selected as appropriate; keep clear of moving fans and belts.

steps.title: Establish the required operating conditions
steps.body: Bring the engine to normal operating temperature. Connect the service unit as directed, select the lowest temperature, disable dual operation if fitted, set high blower and fresh air, and request A/C operation. Use the prescribed open-window and hood setup for this vehicle.

steps.title: Confirm the system can be tested
steps.body: Check that the compressor and cooling fans operate as directed. Allow high- and low-side readings to settle or repeat in a stable cycle. Record ambient temperature and both pressures; use the average where the procedure calls for it.

steps.title: Read the correct pressure charts together
steps.body: Use the 21–38°C (70–100°F) chart set or the hotter-condition chart set as appropriate, including its humidity range. Compare high and low readings as a pair. The listed possibilities are diagnostic leads, not automatic orders for a compressor or a refrigerant top-up.

steps.title: Follow the indicated cause
steps.body: Investigate airflow, engine overheating, control connections, restrictions or leakage as the test results require. Low charge and overcharge are different possible faults. A sensor, wiring or control problem can also interrupt compressor operation.

steps.title: Use a targeted leak test when justified
steps.body: If compressor-shaft leakage is suspected, use the dedicated compressor test. It requires recovery, disconnection and adapters before an isolated test charge, followed by electronic leak detection and recovery again. Its isolated test charge is a dedicated leak-test setup, not a recipe for recharging the whole vehicle.

steps.title: Repair, service and verify the complete system
steps.body: For work that opens the circuit, follow refrigerant identification, recovery, evacuation, oil-accounting and charging instructions with the correct equipment. Use the actual vehicle charge specification, then repeat the applicable performance check to confirm the original concern is resolved.

watchFor.title: A low-side gauge alone is being used to decide the charge
watchFor.body: The performance procedure evaluates both sides under specified conditions. A single reading does not establish a correct refrigerant quantity.

watchFor.title: Pressure suggests more than one possible cause
watchFor.body: Use the follow-on tests to distinguish the possibilities instead of replacing the first component named in the table.

watchFor.title: Refrigerant purity is uncertain
watchFor.body: Identify it before recovery. Contamination requires the designated handling equipment and procedure rather than mixing it into ordinary recovery supplies.

notes: The hotter-condition charts cover 38–49°C (100–120°F); do not extrapolate a plotted limit beyond its stated range.
The compressor leak test specifies an R-134a electronic detector certified to SAE J2791. Its test charge and adapter setup must not be used as a general recharge recipe.
Recovery/evacuation uses both service ports. The linked procedure specifically rules out recovering only through the low-side port.

procedures.purpose: Run the 2.3L performance test and use its pressure charts.
Run the 3.7L performance test and use its pressure charts.
Run the 5.0L performance test and use its pressure charts.
Test a suspected external compressor-shaft leak with the specified isolated setup.
Identify, recover, evacuate and charge the system using the required service process.

guides.title: EcoBoost charge-air cooler: clean only when it needs it
guides.summary: Understand the off-car cleaning process, protect the intake from debris, and complete the required leak test before the cooler goes back in.

applicability.equipment: 2.3L EcoBoost charge-air cooler; requires removal and controlled pressure-test equipment.

guides.introduction: The charge-air cooler, often called the CAC, is part of the pressurized air path between the turbocharger and the engine. This cleaning procedure deals with contamination inside the removed cooler. It involves draining contaminants, washing and rinsing, drying, and then checking that the cooler still holds pressure. The removal-and-installation procedure directs inspection and cleaning when needed; it does not give this job a recurring service interval.
guides.why: Cleaning and sealing are both important to the completed job. Contamination has to leave the cooler, and the cleaned assembly has to pass its leak test before installation. Debris introduced while working on the intake can damage the turbocharger compressor, so a careful removal and clean connections matter as much as the wash itself.

when.summary: When inspection confirms that the removed 2.3L charge-air cooler needs cleaning, or the repair procedure requires it.
notes: This is condition-based work. The procedure does not prescribe periodic CAC washing or automatic cleaning for a low-boost complaint.
Arrange removal, drying, pressure testing and reinstallation as one complete job. Cleaning without the required leak test leaves the procedure unfinished.

prepare.title: Plan safe access and intake protection
prepare.detail: Removal uses a hoist and includes the active grille shutter and lower radiator support bracket. Follow the linked removal procedure. Keep dirt and loose particles out of all opened turbocharger and intake connections.

prepare.title: Have the right cleaning materials
prepare.detail: The procedure names a commercially available detergent such as Simple Green Pro HD or equivalent, used to its manufacturer’s instructions. Metal brake-parts cleaner is specified for the joint clamp areas and connections; keep that task distinct from the detergent wash inside the cooler.

prepare.title: Arrange a suitable leak-test kit
prepare.detail: A commercial charge-air cooler tester, such as the listed 351-CAS type or equivalent, is needed after cleaning. The operator must be able to apply the specified pressure slowly and measure loss accurately. A shop with this equipment is the appropriate next step if it is not available.

steps.title: Remove the assembly using its own procedure
steps.body: Follow [Charge Air Cooler removal and installation](#/document/G1675707), including the sensor connector, inlet and outlet tubes, support and mounting sequence. Once removed, take the boost-pressure sensor and its screw out of the cooler as directed by the cleaning procedure. Protect the opened intake throughout the work.

steps.title: Drain contamination and prepare the connections
steps.body:
Drain coolant, fuel, oil or other contaminants before washing. Clean the specified joint clamp areas and turbocharger, engine and CAC connections. Lay the cooler flat with its inlet and outlet pointing upward.

> **NOTE:** Do not use a high-pressure power washer; it can damage the cooler.

steps.title: Wash, agitate and rinse until the discharge is clear
steps.body: Add the specified type of detergent according to its instructions, then fill with water to **40% of the cooler’s volume**. Cap or plug the openings before agitation. Raise one end and agitate by hand for at least **five minutes**, then raise the other end and repeat for at least **five minutes**. Drain and rinse thoroughly with clean water. Repeat the cleaning cycle until the rinse contains no contaminants.

steps.title: Let it air-dry and prepare the pressure test
steps.body: Allow the cooler to air-dry. Reinstall the boost-pressure sensor and its screw at **44 lb.in (5 Nm)**. Install the commercial tester according to its instructions and tighten the tester clamps to **44 lb.in (5 Nm)**. These values belong to the named sensor and test connections; the vehicle’s inlet and outlet tube clamps have their own installation specification.

steps.title: Verify pressure loss before deciding to reuse it
steps.body:
> **WARNING:** Never exceed the specified pressure. Too much pressure can eject the test adapter or damage the cooler and cause serious injury.

Apply air slowly to **21.8 psi (150 kPa)**. Let the cooler stand for a few minutes and note the pressure loss, then release the pressure. Repeat until **three consecutive tests** show approximately the same drop. If loss exceeds **1.5 psi (10 kPa) per minute**, the procedure calls for a new cooler.

steps.title: Reinstall the assembly only after the required checks
steps.body: Complete the linked removal-and-installation procedure after cleaning, drying and the leak test. Its connection-cleaning instructions, illustrated mounting order and individual fastener torques remain part of the job. Record what contamination was found and the verified pressure-loss result so the next repair decision has useful evidence.

watchFor.title: Contaminants continuing to appear in rinse water
watchFor.body: The cleaning procedure calls for another wash-and-rinse cycle until the discharge is free of contaminants.

watchFor.title: Pressure loss beyond the stated limit
watchFor.body: A cleaned cooler that exceeds the verified leak limit is a replacement case in this procedure.

watchFor.title: Particles near open intake connections
watchFor.body: Even small particles can damage turbocharger compressor vanes. Protect the intake while parts are detached and inspect components before assembly.

notes: The cleaning pressure test must be completed before installation; washing alone is not the complete service.
This guide describes the 2.3L EcoBoost CAC only. It does not apply its test pressure or cleaning method to an engine coolant radiator or transmission cooler.
The illustration is from CAC removal and installation. Its numbered arrows describe mounting movements, not the detergent-cleaning sequence.

procedures.purpose: Follow the complete detergent cleaning, drying and mandatory pressure-loss test.
Remove and reinstall the 2.3L cooler with its illustrations and connection-specific torques.
Use the correct lifting points and supports for the removal work.

guides.title: Driveline vibration: measure before changing parts
guides.summary: Separate a repeatable road-speed vibration from a guess, inspect the shaft and joints, then use runout measurements to choose the next check.

applicability.equipment: Use the specifications for the fitted transmission, driveshaft and flange arrangement.

guides.introduction: The driveshaft carries rotation from the transmission to the rear axle. Its joints and center support have to allow that rotation without binding, excessive movement or a distorted path. Runout is the amount the shaft wanders as it turns, measured with a dial indicator. Balance is a different check involving how mass is distributed around the rotating assembly. Keeping those ideas separate makes a vibration investigation much more useful.
guides.why: The diagnostic chart lists several possible causes of a cruising-speed vibration: joints, the center support, flange fasteners, runout, balance and driveline angles. Adding a weight or replacing the shaft before checking that list can leave the actual problem in place. A repeatable symptom and recorded measurements give each decision a reason.

when.summary: When a repeatable driveline vibration, rumble or shudder remains after an initial inspection, or diagnosis calls for runout checks.
notes: This is symptom-led diagnosis, not a balancing or shaft-replacement mileage interval.
Static inspection and hand-rotated measurements come before the specialized balancing branches. Use the full procedure and a suitably equipped workshop for balancing work.

prepare.title: Preserve a useful starting point
prepare.detail: Before making adjustments, document the road speed and conditions that reproduce the concern. The runout procedure says not to alter tire pressure or vehicle load before its initial road test; record the starting condition rather than changing several variables at once.

prepare.title: Set up support and measuring equipment
prepare.detail:
Use the specified type of holding fixture and dial indicator, such as tool 100-002. The procedure requires the shaft to stay close to its curb-weight position while supported.

> **WARNING:** Never work underneath a vehicle supported only by a jack. Use the correct lifting points and the prescribed stands or hoist arrangement.

prepare.title: Identify the actual shaft configuration
prepare.detail: Know whether the shaft has one or multiple sections and identify its flange type. If angle checks are needed, use the engine/transmission-specific values in [Driveshaft specifications](#/document/G2214897), rather than substituting an angle from another variant.

steps.title: Reproduce and describe the concern
steps.body: Start with a visual check, then have the symptom verified during an appropriate road test. Note whether it follows road speed and whether it appears at cruise, acceleration or coast. Use the [Driveshaft diagnostic chart](#/document/G2214728) to select the matching branch instead of calling every tremor a balance problem.

steps.title: Inspect the shaft, joints and support
steps.body: Look for shaft damage, unwanted undercoating, missing balance weights and poorly seated joints. With the vehicle correctly supported, the inspection procedure rotates the shaft slowly by hand to check for binding and end play. The diagnostic chart also checks the center support for damage, wear or rough operation and the axle flange fasteners for looseness.

steps.title: Correct an identified fault and recheck
steps.body: Follow the relevant repair procedure for the specific defect. Removal, joint or shaft replacement and flange fastener work each have their own requirements. After a correction, recheck at the road-test speed that reproduced the vibration. This preserves the link between the observed fault and the result of the repair.

steps.title: Measure runout at each required position
steps.body: If the vibration remains, fit the dial indicator and rotate the driveshaft by turning the axle as directed. Measure at the **front, center and rear**; on a multi-piece shaft, measure those positions on each section. The linked specifications list **0.6 mm (0.024 in)** for driveshaft runout. Record each position separately so a rear-only result is not confused with a shaft-wide problem.

steps.title: Use the pattern of measurements
steps.body: The procedure calls for shaft replacement when front or center runout exceeds the specification. A rear-only excess leads to its index-marked flange recheck, which helps distinguish shaft eccentricity from a flange or pinion problem. Follow that complete branch, preserving the index marks and correct reassembly details. If all runout points meet the specification but vibration remains, continue to the balance or angle checks indicated by the diagnosis.

steps.title: Keep balancing and angle work controlled
steps.body: The electronic balancing branch uses an accelerometer, a photo-tachometer and the specified vehicle measurement equipment to select and verify corrections. Arrange that work with a shop that can perform the full procedure. For an angle concern, use [Driveshaft Angle Measurement](#/document/G2214729) and the correct variant specifications. Recheck the original symptom after the final correction.

watchFor.title: A damaged shaft, rough joint or worn support
watchFor.body: These are inspection findings to address through the matching repair branch, rather than reasons to add a balance weight.

watchFor.title: Only the rear measurement is out of range
watchFor.body: The index-marked recheck is there to separate possible sources. Preserve the measurements and marks before components are moved.

watchFor.title: Shudder associated with acceleration
watchFor.body: The symptom chart includes driveline angles and binding or damaged joints. That pattern deserves its own branch rather than an automatic balancing operation.

notes: Have balancing performed by a workshop with the equipment and experience required for the fitted shaft and flange arrangement.
The illustration is the inspection view of a multi-piece driveshaft. Confirm the fitted shaft before following any assembly-specific direction.

procedures.purpose: Choose the correct clunk, shudder, cruise-vibration or noise diagnostic branch.
Follow the complete inspection, runout, indexed recheck and specialist balancing instructions.
Check the runout limit, engine/transmission angle values and fastener specifications.
Measure driveline angles with the specified setup and fitted-joint branch.
Review the designated lifting points and support precautions.

guides.title: 6R80 cooler backflushing: protect a repaired transmission
guides.summary: Understand when the cooler and lines need cleaning, why a heated flusher is required, and how contamination checks fit into the complete repair.

applicability.equipment: 6R80 automatic transmission only; specialized transmission-cooling-system service.

guides.introduction: The automatic transmission sends fluid through an external cooler in front of the radiator and then receives it back through the cooler tubes. The cooler releases heat to the passing air. When transmission contamination has been confirmed, the cooler and tubes are part of the repair because material left in that path can return to the repaired unit. The workshop procedure also requires this cleaning whenever the transmission is overhauled or replaced.
guides.why: A rebuilt or replacement transmission still shares its fluid circuit with the existing cooler and tubes. The specified process uses heated, pulsed fluid, filtration and air purging to clean that circuit. A basic fluid exchange or an additive does not satisfy those equipment and process requirements.

when.summary: After transmission overhaul or replacement, or when confirmed contamination requires cooler-and-line cleaning as part of repair.
notes: This is repair-triggered work for the 6R80 automatic, not a routine mileage-based transmission flush.

The diagnostic article calls for repair and cooler/tube cleaning when contamination or transmission failure is confirmed by sediment in the pan. An overheating complaint alone first requires diagnosis of leaks, damage, restriction and fluid level.

prepare.title: Confirm why the work is needed
prepare.detail: Use [Transmission Cooling diagnosis](#/document/G1694304) to establish the concern and the required repair. Confirm the fitted transmission is the 6R80; this process is not an MT82 manual-gearbox service.

prepare.title: Choose a shop with the specified equipment
prepare.detail: The flusher must maintain fluid at **140°F (60°C) or above**, pulsate the fluid, have a GPM flow meter and twin magnetic filters, and be able to air-purge before and after flushing. If equipment meeting those requirements is unavailable, the procedure calls for replacement of the cooler or coolers and hand-cleaning of the lines.

prepare.title: Use the specified fluid and no extra cleaner
prepare.detail: The procedure specifies **Motorcraft MERCON LV Automatic Transmission Fluid, XT-10-QLVC, WSS-M2C938-A**. It prohibits supplemental transmission additives and cleaning agents because they can cause internal component failure.

steps.title: Make the cooler part of the confirmed repair plan
steps.body: Before connecting equipment, establish whether this is an overhaul, a replacement or a contamination repair. Inspect the cooler and tubes for leaks, crushed sections or plugging as directed by the diagnostic chart. Repair or replace defective components through the appropriate repair procedure; do not assume that flushing repairs physical damage.

steps.title: Prepare the heated flusher
steps.body: Check and top off its supply with the specified transmission fluid. Switch on the heater and allow **15–30 minutes** for the fluid to reach **60°C (140°F)** before use. Confirm that the equipment provides every required feature, including the filters and pre/post-flush air purge.

steps.title: Identify inlet and outlet before connecting lines
steps.body: Use the [Transmission Cooling component-location article](#/document/G1694297) and choose its diagram for the fitted engine. Install the line adapters. The cleaning procedure connects the flusher’s **red line to the cooler inlet tube** and its **blue line to the outlet tube**. Use the equipment instructions for the initial air purge before starting the flush.

steps.title: Complete both flushing directions
steps.body: Backflush for **10–15 minutes**, then flush in the normal flow direction for another **10–15 minutes**. These are two specified stages of the cooler-cleaning procedure. Keep the work within the heated flusher manufacturer’s operating instructions.

steps.title: Use the inspection-filter branch when fitted
steps.body: If the flusher has the inspection micron filter described in the procedure, remove and clean its **Oberg 28-micron filter**, reinstall it, then backflush for **five minutes**. Remove and inspect it again. If debris or contamination is present, repeat that cleaning, five-minute backflush and inspection cycle. This branch depends on the actual equipment fitted.

steps.title: Purge, complete assembly and check the vehicle fluid level
steps.body: Perform the final air purge according to the equipment instructions. Complete the cooler and line repair or reassembly, then use the [6R80 Transmission Fluid Level Check](#/document/G1692053) as part of returning the vehicle to service. It uses scan-tool fluid temperature and the indicator’s specified area. The flusher’s heating temperature is not the vehicle’s fluid-level checking temperature.

watchFor.title: Debris returning at the inspection filter
watchFor.body: The specified inspection-filter branch repeats while contamination remains. Keep that result with the repair record rather than ending the process after a single timed pass.

watchFor.title: Leaking, crushed or restricted cooler tubes
watchFor.body: The diagnostic chart treats these as causes that require component service or replacement as appropriate; cleaning does not establish that a damaged part is serviceable.

watchFor.title: A fluid level that has not been verified
watchFor.body: The 6R80 level check has a specified temperature and reading method. Low fluid can cause internal failure, and the procedure says not to drive the vehicle with a low transmission-fluid level.

notes: A normal fluid-and-filter service and this post-repair cooler cleaning have different triggers and equipment requirements. Do not add this procedure to every oil-change or transmission-service visit.

Use the tube-access article for the fitted engine when the repair requires disconnection or tube replacement. The routing and access work vary by engine; the illustration is not a flushing connection diagram.
The prescribed connection colors describe the flusher hoses. Identify the vehicle inlet and outlet from the correct component diagram rather than assuming the drawing colors are physical hose colors.

procedures.purpose: Confirm cooling-system symptoms and the contamination or overhaul trigger for cleaning.
Follow the required heated backflush, forward-flush, inspection and purge sequence.
Follow 2.3L tube access, seals and reassembly details if the repair requires tube removal or replacement.
Follow 3.7L tube access, seals and reassembly details if the repair requires tube removal or replacement.
Follow 5.0L tube access, seals and reassembly details if the repair requires tube removal or replacement.
Identify inlet and outlet tubes using the diagram for the fitted engine.
Understand the external cooler and its fluid path.
Complete the temperature-controlled 6R80 fluid-level check with the specified indicator area.

guides.title: Corrosion protection: restore the barriers that keep water out
guides.summary: Inspect damaged seam sealer, underbody protection and repaired cavities, then choose the right restoration process.
guides.introduction: The body has several layers of protection doing different jobs. Seam sealer closes joints between panels. Underbody coating protects exposed surfaces. Cavity treatment reaches enclosed areas that a brush cannot. Keeping these barriers intact matters just as much as keeping the outside paint looking good, especially where a repair or scrape has disturbed them.
guides.why: Water and dirt can enter an open seam or remain against unprotected metal. Restoring the correct barrier helps limit corrosion and can also prevent water, dust, noise or fumes finding a route into the cabin. A fresh coating is only useful when the surface underneath has been properly inspected and prepared.

when.summary: Inspect exposed metal, damaged coatings or open seams; restore protection as part of the affected repair.
notes: This is condition-based care and repair follow-up, not an instruction to recoat the whole car at a fixed mileage.
Door drainage is part of the regular body check. Additional coating must not close those drains.

prepare.title: Make the surface visible
prepare.detail: Clean away dirt and inspect underbody areas using appropriate vehicle support. Record damaged seams, exposed edges and previous repair areas before deciding what needs treatment.

prepare.title: Identify the protection layer
prepare.detail: Seam sealer, exterior undercoating and internal cavity wax have different jobs. Choose the procedure and material for the location rather than using one aerosol for everything.

prepare.title: Plan repair and application together
prepare.detail: Welding, metal repair and refinishing come before the specified protective treatments. Spraying enclosed areas needs the correct coating gun or cavity wand, ventilation and product-specific protective equipment.

steps.title: Inspect before covering anything
steps.body: Look for broken or missing sealer, bare metal and damaged coating around panel joints and exposed edges. Have corrosion and the underlying metal assessed before applying a new layer. Covering a damaged area does not establish that the metal is sound.

steps.title: Restore the joint or metal first
steps.body: Deal with the damaged panel or joint as required. The sealing guide calls for damaged originally sealed joints to be resealed. Select a compatible, flexible, paintable sealer and follow its application and curing instructions.

steps.title: Prepare a clean surface
steps.body: The corrosion-protection procedure requires removal of dirt, oil, wax and grease before coating. Use the specified preparation process and compatible materials; the coating is not a substitute for surface cleaning.

steps.title: Protect exposed and enclosed areas differently
steps.body: Apply the specified exterior protection after the relevant welding and refinishing work. Treat internal cavities with the appropriate rust inhibitor and wand so the material reaches hidden surfaces. The linked article explains the separate equipment and application settings; these products are not weld-through coatings.

steps.title: Keep drainage paths open
steps.body: Check the bottom of doors and other intended water outlets after treatment. The goal is to protect the metal while still letting water escape. Remove unintended overspray using the compatible cleanup method specified for the product and surface.

steps.title: Document the repair and check it again
steps.body: Keep photos of the treated area and record the product and repair performed. During later body checks, look for lifted coating, reopened seams, trapped dirt or recurring moisture so an application problem can be caught early.

watchFor.title: Swollen seams or metal that appears weakened
watchFor.body: A coating alone cannot repair a structurally damaged panel. Have the extent of corrosion assessed before deciding on cosmetic treatment.

watchFor.title: Water that remains inside a door
watchFor.body: Check the intended drain openings and the water path. Adding more sealant can make the problem worse if it closes an outlet.

watchFor.title: Repeated rust at the same repaired edge
watchFor.body: Review surface preparation, the underlying repair and coverage of hidden faces rather than continually coating over the visible spot.

notes: The hero shows underbody seam locations. Some drawings in the corrosion-treatment article are generic application examples; they are not exact access-point maps for every Mustang panel.
Do not use this coating procedure to lubricate suspension bushings or treat friction surfaces. The material and location must match the job.

procedures.purpose: Identify the roles and typical locations of seam sealers, adhesives and underbody protection.
Restore exterior corrosion protection and internal cavity treatment with the correct preparation and application process.

guides.title: How to replace a head gasket on the 3.7L V6
guides.summary: Find the head gasket, understand what sits above it, and follow the job from intake and valve-cover removal through lifting the cylinder head, fitting the new gasket, rebuilding the timing and checking the repair.

applicability.equipment: Factory 3.7L Duratec V6 with original-style cylinder-head fasteners. Confirm VIN and current Ford instructions; later model years and aftermarket stud kits are not covered.

guides.introduction:
**The head gasket is the thin sealing layer between the cylinder head and the engine block. You replace it by lifting the complete cylinder head off the block—not by removing the valve cover alone.** This V6 has two cylinder heads and two head gaskets, one for each bank. Diagnose which bank needs work before dismantling it.

The **valve cover** is the lid at the top of the head. Its **valve-cover gasket** keeps oil inside that lid. Under the lid are the camshafts and valve gear. The **cylinder head** is the substantial casting underneath those parts. The **head gasket** is below that casting. The **engine block** below the head gasket contains the cylinders and pistons. The block stays in the car for the head-removal procedure described here; this is not an instruction to split the block or remove the crankshaft.

The **upper and lower intake manifolds** are the air passages feeding the heads. They are separate parts, not an “upper block.” If a large piece on top of the engine is what you mean by the upper block, identify it using those names before loosening anything. I want us looking at the same part, not merely agreeing that it is large and inconvenient.

**Why the front of the engine also comes apart:** the timing chains connect the crankshaft in the block to the camshafts in the heads. Ford’s access route removes both valve covers and the front cover, releases the timing-chain/VCT assembly, then removes the affected bank’s camshafts before lifting that head. Removing a valve cover does not disconnect that timing drive.

**Scope:** 2015 U.S. Mustang, factory 3.7L V6 and original-style head bolts, using the supplied 303-01B procedures. LH means the vehicle’s left when facing forward from the driver’s seat; RH means its right. On this U.S. car, LH is the driver’s side. The later revision printed on the supplied head procedures is September 16, 2022; it does not establish applicability to other model years or stud kits.

The access operations and reassembly instructions are written out below. Keep the linked Ford illustrations beside them for the physical bolt positions, tool seating, belt routing and bank-specific timing marks. Those location drawings remain required references; a conceptual diagram is not a substitute for identifying a real fastener.
guides.why: The replacement gasket needs flat, clean, undamaged mating faces, the right fasteners and correct tightening. The timing must then be rebuilt correctly, and the fault that caused overheating or leakage must be resolved. A new gasket cannot straighten a warped head or repair a cracked casting. I treat diagnosis, access, sealing, timing and final checks as separate parts of one repair.

when.summary: Do this repair after diagnosis identifies a failed head-to-block seal or after related head work requires a new gasket. It is not scheduled maintenance and has no routine mileage interval.
notes: An overheating event, persistent coolant loss or a misfire is a reason to diagnose—not proof that the gasket is the cause. Identify the affected bank and the failure path before buying parts.

This is specialist engine work involving valve timing, precision measurement and a large number of dependent procedures. Arrange a machine shop for casting assessment and a capable technician for any timing or measurement work outside your equipment or experience.

Do not start or crank an engine suspected of containing liquid in a cylinder. Do not run an overheating engine just to complete the normal fuel-pressure-release routine; obtain the correct non-running isolation method first.

prepare.title: Know the route before taking anything apart
prepare.detail:
Read the six job phases below once from beginning to end. Open the matching [LH head](#/document/G1681515) or [RH head](#/document/G1681516) drawings, plus the [front-cover bolt map](#/document/G1681517), [camshaft cap maps](#/document/G1681512), [VCT assembly illustrations](#/document/G1681532) and [primary-chain marks](#/document/G1681528). The written steps are here; the drawings identify the actual locations.

The work removes **both valve covers for front-cover access**, even when only one head gasket is being replaced. It removes the camshafts and head only on the diagnosed bank unless the diagnosis calls for both heads. Never start the engine at a linked subprocedure’s “road test” endpoint while this larger job is unfinished.

prepare.title: Have the measurement and timing equipment ready
prepare.detail:
| Equipment | Why it belongs on the bench |
| --- | --- |
| Suitable hoist, approved support points and protected lifting help for the head | Access and safe handling; follow [100-02](#/document/G1663631). |
| Calibrated torque wrenches covering the low and higher ranges, plus a torque-angle gauge | Small bolts use Nm/lb-in values; head bolts also require angle stages. |
| Ford 303-1248 camshaft holding tools and 303-1530 chain-tensioner hold-down tool, or verified application equivalents | Control camshaft position and the secondary tensioner. |
| Calibrated straightedge and feeler gauges | Head/block flatness and valve-clearance work. A workshop ruler is not a calibrated straightedge. |
| Pulley puller, strap wrench and the specified seal/pulley installers | The [front-seal route](#/document/G1681513) lists 303-102, 303-1251, 303-335 and 303-409. |
| Front-cover alignment pins and coolant-pipe seal tooling | [Front cover](#/document/G1681517): 307-399, 205-150 and 205-153. |
